claims.text: Exceptional resistance to combined wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys arises from mechanically triggered formation of a continuous, self-healing nanocrystalline oxide layer.
Compositional complexity promotes dynamic segregation of oxidation-active elements to mechanically stressed surfaces.
The segregated oxidation-active elements rapidly form a protective film that mitigates both mechanical removal and localized corrosion.
Localized mechanical stress accelerates migration of oxidation-prone elements to the alloy surface.
Migrated oxidation-prone elements form a dense, adherent oxide at the surface.
The surface oxide reduces mechanical material loss by acting as a mechanically robust glaze.
The surface oxide inhibits corrosion by acting as a chemical barrier.
The high-entropy effect ensures uniform distribution of oxidation-active elements.
Uniform elemental distribution promotes continuous oxide-film regeneration after mechanical disruption.
Relative to a conventional alloy with similar bulk mechanical properties, the high-entropy alloy will exhibit lower overall material loss during tribocorrosion.
The high-entropy alloy will maintain a more consistent or slightly thickening protective oxide layer during tribocorrosion.
The high-entropy alloy will develop shallower and narrower wear tracks than the conventional-alloy baseline.
The high-entropy alloy will exhibit lower corrosion current density under simultaneous mechanical stress than the conventional-alloy baseline.
The high-entropy alloy will exhibit improved passivation under simultaneous mechanical stress.
A compositionally simpler conventional alloy will form a less uniform and less robust oxide film under matched tribocorrosion conditions.
The less uniform and less robust oxide film on the conventional alloy will cause greater degradation under matched tribocorrosion conditions.
The proposed protective mechanism will operate at moderate wear loads and corrosive intensities when oxide reformation keeps pace with film disruption.
At extremely high loads or in sufficiently aggressive electrolytes, oxide regeneration will fail to keep pace with disruption and degradation will accelerate.
